text: Welcome, investors, to the Absolute Return Podcast, your source for stock market analysis,
global macro musings, and hedge fund investment strategies. Your hosts, Julian Klamaczko and
Michael Kesslering aim to bring you the knowledge and analysis you need to become a more intelligent
and wealthier investor. This episode is brought to you by Accelerate Financial Technologies.
Accelerate because performance matters. Find out more at AccelerateShares.com.
Hey, everybody. Welcome to the Absolute Return Podcast. On today's show, we welcome special
guest, ARC Macro's founder and chief economist Dylan Smith. Having served as an economist at
Goldman Sachs and Rosenberg Research, and later as a private market consultant at McKinsey,
Dylan understands exactly how macroforces translate into the long horizon illiquid world of private
equity and alternatives. On the show, we discuss the current conflict in Iran and its effect on
inflation, persistent government deficit spending, and the implications for bond investors,
what asset class he is most worried about, which segment to the market provides the most
attractive mispricing, and more. With no further ado, here's our show on inflation, war,
and the new market regime with ARC macro founder Dylan Smith.
Hey, Dylan. Welcome to the show. How are you today?
Thanks so much for having me, Julian. I'm very well today. Thank you.
Great. Killing in from beautiful Toronto. Unfortunately, didn't make the playoffs this
year, which I guess is as to be expected, but hopeful for next year. Let's add your macro
specialist at ARC macro, and there's obviously a ton going on right now in particular for context,
April 20th. On again, off again, Middle East conflict with Iran, and oil prices going crazy,
particularly today and over the past several weeks, and equities volatile, credits interesting,
commodities interesting, so a ton to chat about currently, but I wanted to set the stage
focusing on the current macro regime and your view of it.
Yeah. I think a regime is a good place to start, because that's really how we try to think about
the world at ARC macro, and maybe just to give you a bit of context on how we do macro and how
we think we do it a bit differently. We really like to think about, for all the things you've
just described about the world moving very, very fast and markets repricing on the strength of a
single tweet or truth posts very quickly, we try to look through that a little bit. We're more
focused on longer-haul portfolios, institutions managing across public and private markets,
where you're trying to take a view on the world that is a bit more durable than how a
shorter-term trader or a hedge fund might think about playing the markets. This is more about
how do you create long-term value, and how does a macro, good macro thinking fit into that.
The way that we approach that is, we really try and distill all the data down from macro data,
alternative sources, market data, into really three main factors. What's activity doing? What
does growth look like? What's happening in the real economy? Are firms expanding production?
Is investment happening or not? Then what are prices doing? That's really about inflation,
high or low, but we tend to look at that on quite a disaggregated industry level.
What are financial conditions doing? Are they enabling growth or not? Interest rates are high
or low? Are spreads high or low? What type of impulses are imparting on the economy?
When you can simplify it down to just those factors, there's only a finite number of combinations you
can have in terms of, if you think about stuff being a few standard deviations above or below
the historical trend, you can start to package the economy into a few different states. We already
come up with seven that we think are fundamental. I won't go through all seven. I'll tell you in
a second which one we're in now. What's useful about that is then you can look at it and say,
okay, different regimes imply different things about different asset classes. In certain regimes,
you'll want to be way overweight in rates or credit. In other regimes, it's more of an equity
risk-on type of macro setup. That already helps you when you look over an entire portfolio to
think about those kind of allocations and that risk management. Right now, we're in a scenario
that we are a regime that we call sluggish. This is mostly talking about the US economy,
but it can probably apply to Canada as well and to most of the world. What's interesting about
this is when we run the data back to, as far back as 1970, 1960, it's a quite unusual regime.
This is where growth is. It's not negative. It's not recessionary, but it's below potential
certainly and below the long run average. It's moderately inflationary, but inflation is not
like spiking. We're not seeing what we saw in 2022. Yet credit conditions are very easy. We've
seen that in equity prices on average over the last few years. Usually, this is a transitionary
regime. Usually, it's fairly short, lasts a year or maybe less. It's what you get as you're either
coming out of a crisis or going into a crisis. Everyone who's feeling that the US economy for
the last two or three years has been kind of teetering on the edge, we're seeing that in the
data as well. That's the regime we've put it in. The difference this time is it's lasted a very
long time. You expected to resolve one way or the other. You've had all the kind of bears
seeing a lot in the data saying a recession is coming. You've seen markets certainly pricing
a different outcome, but there's been constant shocks that every time it looks like it's breaking
one way or the other, something's happened. There was a huge fiscal impulse and a huge amount of
COVID savings that was spanned as the economy was weakening, which prevented a recession.
You got interest rates coming down at just the right time. Then every time the economy looks
like it's going to accelerate, you get some kind of boneheaded policy. This time last year,
financial markets are very excited. Lots of indicators saying things are on the up and then
Liberation Day tariffs hit and put an end to that for a while. It's been the same this year
where we were seeing a lot of good signs in the early part of the year that labor markets are
sampling and even accelerating slightly and improving slightly. Immigration has a lot to
do with that in terms of bringing supply down at the same time that demand is staying solid enough.
You're seeing deal flow pick up in all sorts of industries, capital signs be allocated,
and then there are more shocks happening. Everyone's hands off again.
And so we're back to sluggish. We published a note a week before the war saying it looks like
we're entering what we call the Goldilocks regime, where growth picks up more to its
longer and average inflation. We were worried about upside risk, but weren't seeing a big
inflation surge happening just yet and still easy financial conditions, which is a great time to be
investing and a great time to be in risk on assets especially. Just as we published that,
the invasion, all the strikes happened. And so we're basically back to this in-between regime
where we're waiting for something to resolve one way or the other.
Chaotic foreign policy certainly keeping you on your toes. And with that sluggish macro regime,
it's interesting because you discussed below potential growth in the U.S. economy. And just
like Hope Springs Eternal with Toronto Maple Leafs fans, it seems to be a similar case for
equity investors and the productivity potential of artificial intelligence, which continues to be
the bold thesis, but really hasn't played out in the numbers. And you just hear about amazing
sort of step change available with new releases of Claude or ChatGPT. And it's just not showing up
in the numbers, and it makes you think, is it ever going to show up? But with respect to your
sluggish regime call, what do you think is the most misunderstood macro force in markets today?
That's an interesting one. I mean, that's one you think about. In terms of misunderstood,
I mean, one thing I think gets a fair amount of attention, but I don't think is being thought
about necessarily in the right way by markets is where fiscal policy is right now. So when you do
hear about it reported, it's kind of this sort of very nervous tone on long run fiscal stability,
which I think is valid in most places. You're seeing developed market debt levels kind of
pushing up towards 100% and a little bit beyond. And outside of World War II, that's basically
unprecedented. And so I think markets are right to be long run nervous. And I think there's a
pocket of assets that that affects, but you hear much less about the near term growth impulse that
that's having. If you just kept that in mind, it was very easy to understand why the US has outgrown
Europe and a whole host of other countries, because they've been subject to an enormous
fiscal impulse. It's changed form under Biden. It was a spending impulse under Trump. It's been a
tax-based impulse, but it is large. And it's large enough, I think, to in normal times be
in our language, be pushing the economy out of the sluggish regime if it was allowed to.
And so that's something we think is being underappreciated. It also has inflationary implications,
certainly in the long term, but also in the short term. And that's where we think something a little
bit overlooked is, even before Iran, just the generally inflationary feeling around the US
economy, which I think was being missed by people. And I think we were seeing a lot of
rate cuts priced in. We were seeing the Fed deciding not to prioritize inflation for a while.
I don't think that necessarily puts inflation back at 7%, but I think it can very easy lock in
3.5%, 4% inflation for a couple of years and become very uncomfortable. And so I think that's
something as well that people have been overlooking. No, you mentioned two things that really top of
mind for me, one being persistent deficit spending and implications for the bond market.
And the second inflation, I want to touch on inflation first, because you mentioned the
outbreak of war in Iran, spiking oil prices and commodities. So things certainly went the complete
opposite way of what the Federal Reserve was expecting. Markets had penciled in to rate cuts
this year, and then new chair Kevin Warsh, I think going to have a tough time getting the
FOMC on board with any sort of rate cuts this year. That said, with where oil is in commodity
prices, aluminum, copper, et cetera, what's your outlook for inflation, even if things do settle
down in the Middle East? Yeah, I can easily see core inflation going above 4%, even above 5%.
So I'm pretty nervous about where we are on price levels. There's a few reasons for that.
I mean, if you just take as your starting point a normal oil price shock, and you run some very
basic regressions, what it spits out is that if you see prices, or for every 10% increase in oil
prices, you should get a quarter of a percentage point of headline inflation on that. So if we
sort of extend that to where we are now with, say, a 40%, 50% price spike for three months,
that's going to put you at about a percentage point of inflation, which is what we're starting to see
in the March data. Now, the longer that persists, it kind of gets up to a certain peak level of
more like 2 percentage points. And so that already gives you headline inflation around 5%.
Now, the two big questions are, how is the shock different? And how does it get down to
into core inflation? And I think that's where there's maybe a bit of complacency around. Firstly,
because I think everyone's pricing good news on the straight-off home moves as if,
once it's open, it stays open. I'm not seeing much consciousness of the fact that it might be
permanently told. You might have constant disruptions to traffic in the way that you did around the Red
Sea when the Houthis were attacking ships, saying nothing of insurance costs, it's saying nothing
of the higher costs of storing hydrocarbons in the region because of potential for attacks.
And so I think we should be treating that region as fundamentally potentially unstable at any
point because of how much Iran has learned about its leverage in the region. And so I think that's
one reason to think that if oil prices do start to take down a bit, they don't have very far down
to go because we need a long-proof period before markets can truly normalize around there, or
for infrastructure to be built to kind of de-risk the Gulf a little bit and move
the alternative sources, which is a few years out anyway. So that's one reason. Another reason,
of course, is that it's not just oil. A lot of important byproducts are produced in refineries
in the Gulf that affects fertilizer prices. It affects plastic prices. It affects all sorts of
industrial inputs that other types of oil price shocks haven't had that. So when oil prices surge
because Russian supply was taking off the market, that was just Russian crude supply to certain
regions. It didn't affect fertilizer prices. It didn't affect plastics prices because that was all
being produced in the Gulf. So we're going to see a much broader price hit. We haven't started seeing
it yet, but that's the longer the straight stays closed, the more that comes. And we're hitting
a point where physical shortages in certain parts of the world are going to become a reality
in oil and refined products and fertilizers, and that can send prices even higher. So the shock's
not done yet is one thing. But then the other important thing I think is that
behavior changes. And this is an overlooked thing, but we have a way of looking at the
producer price index data that tells you whether or not firms are expanding or contracting margins.
So it actually separates out what's that physical goods inflation component and what's from
how firms are deciding to adjust a lot of just margin. And we've seen since over the past year,
we've seen margins contracting as the tar shocks have been absorbed along the value chain.
And we know also from company statements and from the page book and other types of data that
that's happening. Now, you're a CEO of some kind of manufacturing firm in the US. You desperately
want to increase prices because you want some margin recovery from that tariff hit, but your
customers aren't letting you. And then all prices spike and you say, guys, sorry, we have to raise
prices. And actually what you're seeing in the data is that not only are prices going up, but
margins are going up too. So there's some margin recovery happening and that's adding into the
sort of inflationary environment beyond what the oil price shock is doing. So I'm not a big believer
in how we measure inflation expectations. I think calling a bunch of consumers and asking them
whether they think inflation will be, it's basically just wherever inflation is now.
But if you survey firms and ask them what are you doing with prices in the next three months,
one year, that's a pretty solid measurement. It's less easily quantifiable, but that's starting
to really move up. And so I think that is why I think there's going to be some broad based
inflation coming through above and beyond what gas prices would do to inflation normally.
And this is within the context of six years, the US inflation being above the 2% target.
And you think about the Trump administration's objective in getting interest rates lower,
getting inflation lower in contrast to some of the chaotic policy, trade war, tariffs,
war in the Middle East, and all of those dynamics move things the opposite way,
as you indicated with your outlook for inflation. So with that said, what are your thoughts on
not only what the Fed can do this year in addition to global central banks,
because you're really seeing this on a global basis. Are they going to be able to
not just cut rates, but I think right now the market's concerned about just keeping rates
stable and not hiking. Yeah. So what we've seen going into the war,
there was an expectation that rates were going to come down a little further.
Now, I think that underestimated inflation risk that was already there, but okay, so the
Fed was close to neutral and it was going to get on its estimate of neutral, and Warsh would come in
and keep Trump happy, say thank you for putting me in the position, might give him a rate cut or two,
and then actually really decide what his policy was for the next few years. That probably wasn't
going to send inflation soaring even if you were worried about inflation risk. As soon as oil prices
crossed 100, those two rates cuts got taken out of market pricing immediately. Although
interesting, the probability of a hike by the end of the year was almost zero also. So everyone
just sort of crowded around this idea that the Fed's going to be a little bit stuck, and the same
with global central banks. The UK easing cycle was priced out, and hikes started to be rising
in for Europe who were facing that gas price shock as well, and are generally more conservative.
What I found very interesting was, given what I've said about inflation and how even with
the straight open, you don't really know that inflation is not going to continue to be quite
high. As soon as we've had these few days where it's announced that it's open before it closes
again, you get a rate cut to be starting to be priced back in for the end of the year. I think
that's kind of interesting, but also probably a bit of an oversight by markets and something I'd
see as kind of an opportunity for anyone operating in that space. But yeah, it's very hard time to
be a central banker when supply shocks hit because you have to be conscious that you might be in a
situation where growth slows, labor markets weaken, and inflation surges. But there was a real lesson
in the supply shock of COVID, which was that if you do not act in a hawkish manner and basically
communicate to markets, we are extremely observant of this risk, and we'll act as soon as we need to.
You start to get an activity kind of responding and inflationary pressure rising outside of the
supply shock. Part of the job of central banks talking is to act tough enough to say, we will
impose pain if we have to, essentially so that they don't have to, so that you don't get this
behavioral type of pricing that I've been talking about. The risk for the US economy is that the
Fed is once again too dovish to focus on transitory shocks. Even though the shock does end up
transitory, it doesn't mean you have to talk about it that way. That's the communication
challenge of that central bank is always facing. Yeah, and it's certainly not unprecedented. You
see what Alan Greenspan did in terms of warning about equity prices. Was that in the late 90s,
but then in the 2000s, keeping rates probably way too low and effectively spurring the housing
bubble, which ended in disaster. I see potentially some of the same mistakes being made. Now, another
dynamic that you mentioned that should certainly be on investors' radar is persistent deficit
spending in the United States. Current deficit, I think around 6% of GDP, which is really unprecedented
outside of war or massive recession. I guess technically there is a war now, but
this spending was happening before that. There seems very little imperative to reduce
that budget deficit. Not only in the US, but you're seeing massive federal government debt
like in Japan and a good case study there. Focusing on the United States economy and the
largest bond market in the world, what, if any, do you think this persistent deficit spending
and exploding government debt throughout the world, is that ever going to have an effect
on the Treasury market? The so-called Minsky moment, if you want to refer to it as that.
Yeah. Well, I find it difficult to see that type of moment happening in the US economy. I don't
think it's impossible, but I think these types of issues, if we learn anything from Japan and other
very large economy debt problems. I've worked on debt blowups in small economies, and that's a
whole different dynamic. It's almost more like a company blogger. But for the US, this enormous
provider of most of the world's liquid financial assets, it's a bit more difficult to see than
happening. The much more likely scenario is just a steady, steady grind towards a worse and worse
situation until something gives either policy-wise or otherwise to deal with that pressure.
If you think about one of the ways out, there's this big deficit. I'm always fascinated when I
speak to politicians about this because I say, do you guys know what you're saying? Why aren't
you acting on this, basically? The answer is always some form of, well, we have immediate
political pressure right now. If this becomes a bigger problem, we'll deal with it then.
And natural termism is not a good mix for this kind of thing because when this becomes a problem,
it's probably too late to properly fix without avoiding some economic pain.
And so, okay, so what are your options to deal with that kind of thing, say if the political
wall eventually emerges to do that? Well, the great way out of it, which is what I think everyone's
hoping for, is that you just get this awesome productivity boom kind of growth surge where
growth picks up like durably to 4%. Tax revenues are just rising on their own. And you can still
spend quite high, but much deficit comes down because of that kind of organic thing. I really
hope that happens. If there's anywhere it is going to happen, it's probably in the US first
because I think adoption of AI by firms is much quicker and there's a sort of culture that
might enable that in the States, whereas if you look at other very highly indebted countries,
say in Europe or in Canada, much more frictions in the economy towards adopting those types of
technologies and so probably would be a little bit more difficult. But you mentioned productivity up
top, and there's the famous quote of, you can see it all around you except in the numbers.
Productivity is something that is very, very hard to measure for one thing and it compounds,
like interest rates do. So a small amount of productivity growth spread across 5 or 10 years
can actually grow the economy in terms of living a lot. But you don't really see it as this big
structural jump in the way that the oil price tripling would really structurally change the
economy very, very quickly. It's a much slower kind of effect. But if you think about how different
the world was 30 years ago and how much more productive we are, like the internet's definitely
done stuff and cloud computing and all these things have definitely changed how we operate
and made us more productive, we've just spent most of that productivity on things.
So that's one thing, maybe there'll be some growth, maybe not. The other way is to actually
deal with the underlying problem, which is that it's about Western developed countries around
a fiscal space. The budgets, there have been years of commitments to welfare spending,
whatever your political views on that affect about them is that they are sticky. They're not
something you can easily adjust through the cycle. In fact, they tend to be pro-cyclical and that
usually you have to send a bit more on welfare when things are getting bad.
And so you see this in the public debate, it's starting to emerge as a serious thing now in
places like Canada and the UK. If you think about what's committed to welfare spending,
what's kind of locked in government spending that you can't really afford and other things in the
US, you add the military on top of that. And your wiggle room actually becomes very, very small.
And since COVID, there's been a huge amount of pressure to spend that wiggle room to support
the economy. I think it's evident in how Trump operates. There was basically no case for a
tax cut money from a pure economic standpoint when he made the tax cuts, but he made them.
We're seeing the Carney government is coming in and we're already putting the economy first in
Canada. It's not bringing spending down very much. There's some right sizing of the public
services, a few other things, but they're going to spend some of the oil windfall and give it back
to consumers. So it's just such an easy thing to do as a politician and just keep the can down to
later. So we're going to negotiate the social contract. We probably should be doing it.
That's not going to happen. It's too political difficult. So your third way out is to inflate.
It's to allow a certain level of persistently high average inflation to bring down the relative
value of government debt compared to GDP. And so I think bond markets are seeing that. If you look
at where the patient premium is on 20 or 30 year paper, there's a big inflation premium in there.
Because over that time period, I don't think you're going to build on 2% inflation. Probably
going to be 3% or 4%. And it appears with your thesis about central banks potentially running at
hot, which looks like, I mean, politically, perhaps the only way to get it at that quagmire
that they're in. In that scenario, what assets are best positioned to capitalize on that? What
would do the best in that scenario? Yeah, well, that would reverse a very long period of great
performance of fixed income. So we've seen as from the 90s onwards, basically, when central
banks got a hold of inflation, when they started inflation targeting, when they said this is our
main aim, and manage the economy with the goal of keeping inflation stable. And they got a huge
amount of help from Chinese production coming online and really reducing the cost of global goods
production. That's been a great time for bonds. And interest rates got all the way down to a decade
around zero, basically. That holds over, I think. That holds over. And so I think that's,
you've got to find assets that will hold their value through a period of sustained inflation.
And that's equities with pricing problem. And that's part of, I think, why valuations have
picked up a little bit on average in equities. Now, conversely, it'd be interesting to hear
where you think the market is complacent. We spoke about probably the most appreciated risks,
inflation, deficit spending, or commodity prices, supply chain, etc. But are there any hidden
fragilities? There's some known unknowns, unknown unknowns, some stories in the news,
whether it be potential AI bubble, and what happens if that capital expenditure boom reverses.
Should people be worried about private credit? Are there cockroaches there? Is it going to be
another 2008? Even the Canadian housing bubble seems to burst, and no one really cares. And it had
had a very little effect. It gets on Canadian equities or the Canadian economy. Are there
any hidden fragilities in the system or things that you think the market's being complacent on?
Yeah. Well, I think the AI one everyone knows about. I think everyone remembers dark fiber
from the 90s and knows that you can't overbuild. It's difficult to picture based on how much
usage is expanding and all the AI firms are constantly running out of compute.
We don't know where the tax is going. Maybe someone invents just incredibly much more efficient
AI way of doing AI that invalidates half the GPU bull that we've had. Who knows? But I think
everyone kind of understands that that's a risk that's there and that would be pretty negative
for Microsoft materialized. One's that are harder to spot. I think private credit's interesting
because there is a story there, but people are getting it wrong in terms of what the story is.
So I think the current problems we're seeing there is essentially an issue with the retail-focused
private credit model, where we've seen private credit firms have set up semi-liquid funds. They've
tried to attract mostly high net worth retail investors. They've said, look, we aren't performed
banks. This is a boom time. Institutions are doing great. But these investors don't have the
patience of institutional investors. And they're a bit more sensitive to what's in the news. So
they see two or three private credit firms blow up. They call their advisor and they want their
money back. And so we're seeing things gated out. Now, probably defaults won't go up.
And it's possible that some of that will happen in software where private equity is over-indexed
because there will be firms that just get wiped out by AI. There are other firms that will
do incredibly well in ways we don't understand yet. But probably you're dealing with a slightly
higher default environment. Okay, fine. That's cyclical and probably manageable. It doesn't
mean the whole economy blows up. And the other thing about private credit is it's still mostly
institutional and it's locked in. And so even if funds underperform and defaults are higher than
you expect, you just get institutions marking down their book. It's not like this massive
chain of collateral blows up or suddenly the banking systems in big trouble. It's like
returns of pension funds are suboptimal, which is not good for everyone, but it's also not a crisis.
I think what we might be missing a little bit, especially in the US, is collateralization is
back. And it's kind of the bit that's like semi-linked to private credit. It's not purely
about private credit. Some collateralized lending is more in private space. A lot of it's more
actually in the banking space. But there have been a few kind of innovations around market
structure in terms of factoring receivables. And it's murky. This is why there's been some
comparisons to 2008, where it's just hard to say what the kind of leverage chains look like
and where the banks are actually significantly exposed to other financial institutions that
significantly exposed. So if I was like a regulator, I would be looking quite hard,
not at private credit so much as how is the return of pretty high levels of securitization
affecting most of the banking system. The Europeans are on this actually,
but it's bigger in America and it's less regulated in America.
Right. And I think your thoughts on private credit and what's happening there really nails it
if people are going to make the comparison to the GFC. And you got to realize that,
look at Lehman Brothers, it was levered like 30 to one or 50 to one. And these private credit
funds are levered maybe one to one. In addition, you spoke about the matching of assets and liabilities,
whereas Lehman Brothers had the liquidity sector almost immediately as you see in a banking crisis
and in the BDC space, you really don't have that asset liability mismatch, which really
creates the problems when you combine it with leverage. And it is an interesting concern around
CLOs and the structuring of broadly syndicated loans and even private credit loans as a market
that has grown significantly. And I think without a lot of attention and it's sort of
to be seen what's going to happen there, but it's certainly worthwhile monitoring.
Now that said, Dylan, I have one last one for you prior to letting you go. You mentioned
feeding in with your global macro thesis. You mentioned equities with pricing power as good
place to be. Well, with that said, do you see any big asymmetry if you put your asset allocator hat
on? Is there anything that's massively mispriced? Is there any indicators that people aren't paying
attention to? Where's kind of the highest potential opportunity? Well, can I give you an opportunity
and a concern? Yes, definitely. I'll start with a bad one so we can end on a more positive note,
but I'm a little worried about gold. I did some talks at the beginning of the year
and kind of did the classic hands up who thinks this or that asset price will be the best performing
asset price this year. And this was with retail advisors and gold was by far going to be the best
performing asset this year. I've been looking at it kind of ever since and there's something
interesting happening in gold, which is that it is now positively correlated with risk sentiment.
It is a risk asset at the moment. It won't always remain that way, but the scale of the
appreciation in the last two years, the change in the investor base, the interest from retail
and day trading investors at its current level is making it a risk asset. And the reason that
that's a bit concerning is that it is still being held in a lot of portfolios overweight
because of the appreciation as a hedge. So what it's doing is it's basically there's all these
portfolios that have passively increased the allocation to the factors that drive equity
through their gold holdings. And so inflation, and so they're not as well inflation protected as
they think, they're not as well protected to downturns as we think. I mean, if you look at how
gold's traded through the wall, it's well, whenever something inflationary has happened
and oil prices have surged, gold is down. And when the straits open again, somehow gold's up,
even though oil prices are going down, which is not the right way around in terms of holding
gold for geopolitical risk offsets and inflation protection, right? Something else is going on
there. So I'm cautioning people to be a little careful with gold at the moment. If you want to
take the risk, that's fine. But understand it, it's not a hedging asset right now.
In terms of opportunities, I quite like software. I like it as a sort of fresh investment, so
private equity going into new software, theses that integrate a good AI perspective. And I even
like it as an undervalued stock at the moment. And that's just because of how the sell-off happened,
right? It was completely indiscriminate. Some random research firm puts on a note and says,
software's over. Most software firms are pretty quick moving and able to, they're kind of the
first places that deal with these shocks, right? So there are a lot of, I think, high-quality
companies that have made the transition to cloud very effectively, but are now thinking hard about
how to make the transition to AI and how to put AI into their business efficiently.
I do not think LLM solved every problem. I run a small business. I would not trust cloud because
it is good as it is with my entire CRM and my entire finance infrastructure. I might let it do
